{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=longitudinal+persistence+of+interaction-induced+regime+shifts+in+human-AI+dyads+beyond+immediate+session+constraints&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6766938\", \"title\": [\"Epistemic Coprocessors and the Emergence of Stable Human-model Dyads: Toward an Architecture of Asymmetric Human-AI Interaction\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p>Recent generations of Large Language Models have enabled a new form of human–machine interaction: relatively stable epistemic dyads between human actors and probabilistic language systems.&nbsp;</p>\\n<p>This paper introduces the concept of the asymmetric epistemic dyad as a preliminary analytical framework for describing recursive human–model interaction architectures within probabilistic epistemic environments.&nbsp;</p>\\n<p>The paper argues that the decisive transition is not anthropomorphic “machine intelligence,” but the emergence of interaction architectures in which models function as <em>epistemic coprocessors</em>. Within such <em>dyads</em>, meaning integration, normative evaluation, intentional direction, and epistemic responsibility remain located on the human side, while models contribute probabilistic structural processing, recursive reconstruction,&nbsp;semantic variation, and stabilization of extended epistemic operations.&nbsp;</p>\\n<p>The framework distinguishes these interaction architectures from prompting, conventional software augmentation, and earlier models of distributed cognition.&nbsp;</p>\\n<p>The paper does not claim that language models possess consciousness, intentionality, autonomous understanding, or independent epistemic agency. Nor does it claim finalized empirical validation for the proposed framework. The analysis is exploratory, architectural, and conceptual.&nbsp;</p>\\n<p>Its primary contribution lies in defining a conceptual observation and analysis space for investigating long-form recursive human–AI interaction under conditions of sustained epistemic continuity.&nbsp;</p>\\n<p>The document should therefore be understood as an exploratory working framework situated within the broader discourse on human–AI interaction, epistemic infrastructure, and probabilistic cognitive environments.</p></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6766938\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.1335347\", \"title\": [\"Monetary Policy Regime Shifts and Inflation Persistence\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper reports the results of estimating a Markov-Switching New Keynesian (MSNK) model using Bayesian methods. The broadest and best fitting MSNK model is a four-regime model allowing independent changes in the regimes governing monetary policy and the volatility of the shocks. We use the estimates to investigate the mechanisms that lead to a decline in the persistence of inflation. We show that the population moment describing the serial correlation of inflation is a weighted average of the autocorrelation parameters of the exogenous shocks. Changes in the monetary or shock volatility regimes shift weight over these serial correlation parameters and affect the serial correlation properties of inflation. Estimation results indicate that a shift to a monetary regime that reacts more aggressively to inflation reduces the weight on the more persistent shocks, so lowers inflation persistence. Similarly, a shift to the low-volatility regime reduces the weight on the more persistent shocks and also contributes to reducing inflation persistence. Estimates of model-implied inflation persistence indicate that it began rising in the late 1960s and peaked around the Volcker disinflation. The subsequent decline in persistence is due to both a more aggressive monetary policy regime and less volatile shocks.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1335347\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7019258\", \"title\": [\"AI-Human Interaction as Interface: Symbolic Traversal, Subject-Position Effects, and Regime Confusion in the AI-Human Literature\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><div>\\n In this working paper, I develop a methodological framework for studying AI–human interaction as an interface regime rather than as transparent conversation. I examine a recurrent inference pattern in LLM-era scholarship: coherent voice, repair-like sequences, refusal explanations, interpretability cues, and anthropomorphic effects are often treated as baseline conversational properties, and then used to support claims about meaning-making, agency, trust, partnerhood, or relational participation.\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n <br>\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n I call this pattern interface naturalization. Against it, I treat instruction hierarchies, alignment objectives, safety policies, system cards, and interface conventions as manual-layer evidence of the constraint profile that governs output formation. The framework distinguishes substrate-level Symbolic traversal from interface-conditioned centering effects and stabilization patterns under strain. This distinction preserves the descriptive value of transcript analysis while tightening what such evidence can warrant.\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n <br>\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n The paper contributes a regime-aware interpretive standard for AI–human interaction research. It proposes minimal reporting requirements and a diagnostic vocabulary for classifying transcript phenomena across Symbolic traversal, Imaginary-like centering, and Real-type strain management. The aim is not to deny that AI outputs can be socially meaningful, interactionally useful, or affectively satisfying. It is to clarify how claims about conversation, agency, and partnerhood should be evaluated once the interface is treated as constitutive rather than transparent.\\n</div></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7019258\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.54941/ahfe1003558\", \"title\": [\"Beyond the tool vs. teammate debate: Exploring the sidekick metaphor in human-AI dyads\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>From symbiosis to copilot, a wide range of metaphors have been employed to characterize cooperative and collaborative relationships between human and non-human agents (be they software, robots, algorithms, or automated agents of any kind) in support of designing such advanced technologies. Recently, the emergence and rapid commoditization of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms have driven a highly bimodal debate on what metaphor is best to account for AI’s and ML’s new capabilities, particularly when those closely mimic humans’: Is AI a tool or a teammate for humans using the technology? This debate, however, occludes critical elements necessary to practitioners in the fields of human system design. To move past the “tool vs. teammate debate,” we propose an orthogonal metaphor, that of a sidekick, inspired by popular and literary culture, which can both accomplish and facilitate work (i.e., they do, and they help do). The sidekick metaphor was applied to a variety of efforts where it yielded novel design considerations which would have otherwise been unattainable by previous approaches. In this contribution, we report on the debate, describe the sidekick metaphor, and exemplify its application to real-world use cases, in domains such as intelligence analysis, aircraft maintenance, and missile defense.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.54941/ahfe1003558\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "a761ce0a915fec67df982a32f3c720a78d28d3334ccafc70b4a6c29cf0ac47fb", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6766938", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.1335347", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7019258", "doi:10.54941/ahfe1003558"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6766938", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1335347", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7019258", "https://doi.org/10.54941/ahfe1003558"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
